title: Can AI Replace Human Judgment? Medicine, Law, and the Future — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: Leonard shifts the focus from preserving writing-based judgment and developmental opportunities to the profession’s ultimate purpose and outcomes. She suggests that lawyers should not defend cognitively rewarding or identity-forming work merely because it is traditionally human, while offering no direct evidence about verification costs or independent competence.
qs: But if the ultimate question is, how do I help patients have healthier lives?—his conclusion was, I would rather use technology that's more accurate and use my abilities elsewhere.

For me, I was thinking about lawyers and how emotional some of the reactions have been across law to LLMs—at first denial, then an assertion like, I add this edge to my writing that is so unique (and that's what my client wants from me), to really zooming out and asking the question: why do we exist as lawyers in the first place?

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not establish or directly engage the cluster’s central claim that automating junior work threatens expertise reproduction and creates a verification paradox. It instead redirects attention toward new client-interaction capabilities and a broader conception of legal training centred on navigating ambiguity, professional purpose and institutional reform.
qs: Entering the profession right now is such an interesting and, I think, exciting time because you're going to be able to build a new muscle for how to respond to that kind of interaction with potential clients.
It's essential to understand how to argue different positions and unpack subjectivity when it's really unclear.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The excerpt introduces a medical comparison among AI alone, doctors, and AI-assisted doctors as a prompt for considering legal implications. Because it reports no results or conclusions about assistance versus replacement in legal adjudication, it does not establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.
qs: And today, we are going to explore a new study that came out that focuses on ChatGPT and its ability to diagnose different medical conditions and comparing its capacity to do that with doctors and with doctors who used AI.
And on this episode in particular, in other fields that might be analogous and also somewhat different, but from which we can start to learn and think about implications in legal.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source frames cross-disciplinary learning about AI’s implications for law, which is compatible with the cluster’s learning agenda. However, the excerpt reports no study findings and does not advocate lawyer-led deployment, implementation support, experimentation, or governance participation, so its position on the cluster’s engagement-first proposition cannot be determined.
qs: And in particular, we try to connect the dots for people in our profession in the legal industry and field with developments that are happening more broadly in the technology realm.
And on this episode in particular, in other fields that might be analogous and also somewhat different, but from which we can start to learn and think about implications in legal.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s comparison with imperfect human judgment and materially extends it by proposing LLM-based analysis of consistency and fairness across judicial dockets. It also links greater institutional transparency to public confidence, while treating benefits as prospective and leaving ethical safeguards for experimentation unresolved.
qs: You know I'm a big believer that more transparency into how our judicial systems and alternative dispute resolution systems operate—and how they work—is better for growing public confidence in that really fundamental institution.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational change rather than technology alone and materially extends the cluster by identifying expert overconfidence, lawyer-led disciplinary insularity and limited attention to alternative business structures as specific barriers to institutional absorption. Its claims are primarily reasoned observations and predictions, not measured evidence of adoption outcomes.
qs: One of the things I talk about a lot is monodisciplinarity—the fact that all of our systems and organizations have to be owned and led by lawyers means that we miss out on insights from other disciplines.
So there's basically one model, and it might not be the best one for what's coming with this technology.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source broadly accepts outcome-focused AI use rather than defending human expertise or text production for its own sake. It materially extends the cluster by proposing that legal training be redesigned around broader professional purposes and consensus-building, while also reinforcing the cluster’s caution that high-stakes legal experimentation raises unresolved client-protection concerns.
qs: But if the ultimate question is, how do I help patients have healthier lives?—his conclusion was, I would rather use technology that's more accurate and use my abilities elsewhere.
Jen Leonard: Yeah, and I think it goes back to the training piece of what activities and skills we’re prioritizing or including in the toolkit we provide to new lawyers.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of legal AI as organisational change rather than a mere technology purchase and materially extends it by identifying expert overconfidence, lawyer-dominated governance and professional identity as barriers to multidisciplinary innovation and alternative delivery models. Its claims are mainly analogical and anecdotal, not evidence that AI outperforms lawyers.
qs: One of the things I talk about a lot is monodisciplinarity—the fact that all of our systems and organizations have to be owned and led by lawyers means that we miss out on insights from other disciplines.
Somebody who's seasoned and has been around a long time and is sure that there's a right way to do things can be dismissive of a suggestion from a more junior member of the profession.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-centred work-redesign proposition: technology can absorb some cognitively demanding work while lawyers concentrate on strategy, empathy, communication and judgment. It materially extends the cluster by proposing redesigned lawyer training and carefully designed randomized controlled trials and more objective outcome measures, while highlighting legal subjectivity, jurisdictional variation and client protection as constraints on evaluation and deployment.
qs: moment, I pushed through all of these and I am designing randomized control trials for anybody who wants to put these together.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports practitioner-led experimentation before technological certainty by describing bounded, iterative uses of AI for testing presentations and drafting marketing content. It treats AI as a thought partner whose suggestions remain subject to human selection, while its medical analogy is exploratory and supplies no evidence that AI can replace legal judgment.
qs: But the next step is, once you're satisfied with it, feeding it back into the model as a full script and saying, can you think of places where there are additional topics I should be addressing or what questions our audience members would have about each of these points that I make?

kp.k: Medical trial challenges assumptions about human–AI collaboration
kp.d: McCormack reports a study by researchers from Stanford, Beth Israel, and UVA involving 50 physicians—26 attending physicians and 24 residents—from family, internal, or emergency medicine. Physicians were randomized to conventional resources with or without GPT-4, tackling six clinical vignettes within 60 minutes; a separate assessment tested the LLM alone. Blinded experts graded diagnostic reasoning, time per case, and final diagnosis accuracy. The physician groups differed by only two grading points, not statistically significantly, and showed similar time efficiency; the LLM alone performed significantly better. This is reported medical evidence, not a demonstrated result for legal practice.
qs: They recruited 50 physicians—26 attending physicians and 24 residents.
The other group of physicians used only those conventional research resources they were used to, and they tackled six different clinical vignettes within 60 minutes.
There was only a two-point difference in their grading, which was not statistically significant.

The most striking finding, and the reason everyone's talking about it and people are writing about it in the popular press, was that the LLM alone performed significantly better than both groups of physicians.

kp.k: Research lag may obscure newer models' capabilities
kp.d: Leonard says the studied model was a year old and tentatively identifies it as GPT-4.0 Turbo. She speculates that model advances since the research could make the results more pronounced; the transcript provides no newer-model results to establish that possibility.
qs: It was GPT-4.0 Turbo, I think, and they made the point that there's an academic lag in research and advancement of the models.
So we could imagine that the results might be even more pronounced now.

kp.k: Expert overconfidence may obstruct productive AI use
kp.d: McCormack reports that physicians with ChatGPT access sometimes disagreed with and overruled it. Leonard attributes the concept of algorithmic aversion to Ethan Mollick. McCormack analogizes this to senior lawyers dismissing junior colleagues, illustrating it with students whose initially rejected procedural argument succeeded. She predicts that new lawyers comfortable with technology and less certain of their own answers may use it more ambitiously.
qs: What's fascinating about that is the physicians who had access to ChatGPT-4 obviously had the benefit of ChatGPT-4's thinking, but they disagreed with it in many cases.

Ethan Mollick calls it "algorithmic aversion"—if you're an expert, being averse to something that disagrees with you that feels like a machine that would not be as intelligent as you are as an expert.

So I think it's an interesting reminder about experts' instinct to be overconfident in their own judgment—whether it's a technology or a junior person in your profession who has a new way of thinking about it or is using technology in a new way.

kp.k: Professional purpose may outweigh attachment to cognitive work
kp.d: Leonard reports Dr. Adam Rodman's willingness, in a separate interview, to use more accurate technology for patients and redeploy his abilities despite enjoying diagnostic reasoning. She applies this as a question for lawyers: whether professional pride and enjoyment of writing or analytical work should give way to better service and quicker resolution. This is a proposed professional reorientation, not evidence that legal judgment has already been displaced.
qs: But if the ultimate question is, how do I help patients have healthier lives?—his conclusion was, I would rather use technology that's more accurate and use my abilities elsewhere.

What would be the comparable coming-to-terms in our profession of letting go of a little bit of the cognitive work that we really enjoy and value, in service of better services and quicker resolution of legal issues for our clients?

kp.k: Generative AI accelerates drafting and business development
kp.d: Leonard describes uploading presentation screenshots to ChatGPT and obtaining scripts with approximately 90% of her intended content on almost every slide, requiring minor nuanced adjustments. She also used it to anticipate skeptical lawyers' objections and reports lawyers drafting marketing posts and client alerts from public litigation materials. McCormack emphasizes time savings and creative iteration. These are personal experiences and practitioner reports rather than measured productivity findings.
qs: And on almost every slide, with very little information but a little bit of background, it got maybe 90% of the content right.

I deliver presentations to lawyers who tend to be a very skeptical audience, so poke holes in some of the things I'm saying here and then help me come up with assertions to counter those or respond to them or incorporate the things I think are worthwhile into the presentation.

For example, if they've had a successful outcome in litigation, they upload some of the publicly available records of the case and articles, and then saying, "Draft a blog post that I can use and distribute to my clients as a client alert."

kp.k: Lawyer-dominated leadership can exclude alternative business ideas
kp.d: Leonard argues that lawyer ownership and leadership produce monodisciplinarity, encouraging dismissal of insights from finance, marketing, professional development, and court administration. McCormack adds that law schools and firms devote little attention to other business structures and questions whether the prevailing model fits emerging technology. Neither supplies a specific replacement staffing or pricing model.
qs: One of the things I talk about a lot is monodisciplinarity—the fact that all of our systems and organizations have to be owned and led by lawyers means that we miss out on insights from other disciplines.
So there's basically one model, and it might not be the best one for what's coming with this technology.

kp.k: Professional education should reconsider technology-dependent skill needs
kp.d: The hosts discuss Rodman's reported debate about medical education and whether memorization remains appropriate when information tools are available. Leonard contrasts anecdotal executive-MBA chatbot use for course assistance and classroom inquiry with less visible modeling in legal education. She suggests, explicitly as an overgeneralization, that medical faculty's active clinical work may enable faster educational responses than among law faculty not practicing daily. They raise questions about future professional attractiveness rather than predicting enrollment outcomes.
qs: So having to memorize every single thing probably isn't going to be the most important skill.
That's both modeling and substantive use of the technology. I think we don't always see that in legal education or in professional development once we enter practice.

So they may be seeing this unfold in the professional landscape in ways that support their immediate strategic response in the educational realm—something that might be slower to reach law school faculty who are not practicing day to day and aren't seeing this infuse into their work as readily.

kp.k: Efficiency gains could expand service and human engagement
kp.d: Leonard contrasts medicine's insurance-driven efficiency pressures with law's lack of an equivalent third-party driver. She reports Rodman's concern that technology could remove remaining humanity from medicine, but sees legal inefficiency as an opportunity to serve more people and businesses while prioritizing strategic partnership, empathy, and problem solving. McCormack also suggests automation could free professionals to explain findings and communicate with clients or patients. These are conditional opportunities, not observed service-expansion results.
qs: I've always used that as a main reason why we don't innovate more in law: because there is no third party driving efficiencies.
His concern was that these advancing technologies might try to squeeze out the tiny bit of humanity left in medicine.

In legal, I actually think there are exciting opportunities because of how inefficient we are in our profession compared with medicine—how many more people and businesses we could serve, and how the ability to elevate those human skills opens up a huge swath of opportunity in my mind if we could spend a little less time on the things that we think of as cognitively challenging (but that may be depriving many more people of strategic partnership, empathy, and problem solving on their side).

kp.k: AI-informed clients will require new communication skills
kp.d: Leonard anticipates solo and small-firm clients arriving with ChatGPT explanations of their options and preferred strategies, rather than asking lawyers to interpret unfamiliar documents from scratch. McCormack compares this to patients bringing internet diagnoses to doctors and predicts a learning curve for lawyers, with new entrants potentially advantaged in developing communication practices that address technology's limits.
qs: I don't know how that plays out when you're a solo or small practice and your client comes in and says, "I've already talked with ChatGPT. It explained to me what my legal options are. I want you to pursue this one."

It's better communication than lawyers maybe have had to do, but I think new lawyers will have an advantage again because they'll figure out a lot of this in a way that'll make them really good lawyers, in my view.

kp.k: Legal fragmentation complicates consumer-facing information services
kp.d: Discussing the absence of a WebMD-like legal service, McCormack suggests state-specific law makes a national equivalent harder to monetize and tentatively raises unauthorized-practice enforcement as another explanation. Leonard adds that many people have never had a lawyer, so technology would not necessarily replace an existing professional relationship. Both present these as hypotheses, with Leonard also emphasizing federalism.
qs: Whereas in law, there's potentially a different rule of law in each state—50 different answers.
The fact that there's no legal singularity means it's harder to monetize a WebJD.
Maybe because lawyers are better at prosecuting UPL (unauthorized practice of law). I'm not sure.
It’s not a matter of replacing their conversation with a lawyer, because they don't have a lawyer in the first place.

kp.k: Legal AI trials remain proposed rather than completed
kp.d: McCormack describes using Claude to design two randomized controlled trials addressing legal diagnosis and legal decision making, including ethical design and comparisons of efficiency and confidence in results. She plans to discuss the designs with law-faculty contacts and recommends this as a law-school research opportunity, while expressly stating that she does not currently intend to run them herself.
qs: I asked Claude to help me design some randomized control trials for legal diagnosis and for legal decision making. I'm actually designing two different randomized control trials.
I don't have any intention of running them myself right now
I think this is a great project for law schools trying to figure out what all this means, and I'm not aware of anyone doing it.

kp.k: Legal subjectivity complicates evaluation and exposes systemic weaknesses
kp.d: McCormack contrasts medicine's comparatively quantitative orientation with law's contextual judgments about fairness and persuasion, making trial outcomes harder to quantify. She argues that inconsistent subjective answers may themselves be a weakness for people planning lives and businesses. Leonard likewise questions whether interpretive contest should remain central, while acknowledging that language makes standardization difficult. These are methodological concerns and normative arguments, not findings that objective measures have been established.
qs: So much of the currency in justice, like fairness and persuasion, is subjective. That makes it far harder to quantify, and designing a study is a little more complicated.
The fact that you can get different subjective answers from different decision makers in the legal system feels more like a weakness than a strength.
But should the primary objective really be the lawyerly ability to play with language to get different results? Or should we, to your point, develop more standardized approaches?

kp.k: Upstream ambiguity analysis could prevent legal disputes
kp.d: Referring to Adam Unikowski's work, McCormack suggests analyzing statutory or sentencing-guideline ambiguity before codification could reduce disputes. Leonard recommends supplementing training in adversarial interpretation with skills for developing consensus around language before laws are created. The proposed change shifts some professional effort from exploiting ambiguity toward preventing it.
qs: I think it's a lot harder to eliminate ambiguities in language, but as Adam showed, if you were to analyze ambiguity—in his case, it was a sentencing guideline or a statute before it was codified—you might have far fewer disputes.
But it also seems useful to help students and new lawyers think about developing consensus around language in advance of creating laws

kp.k: Closed-case trials could target unmet civil legal need
kp.d: McCormack rejects randomly assigning real defendants to trial or guilty pleas as unethical and proposes closed cases or hypotheticals with complete case details instead. She identifies high-volume eviction and consumer-debt dockets, with similar elements, defenses, and outcomes and many people receiving no legal help, as promising research settings with substantial potential benefit. She acknowledges that these designs would not be identical to large medical trials involving people with the same diagnosis.
qs: Because you can't really say, we're definitely going to go to trial with Client A (who's charged with this particular offense) and Client B we're going to plead guilty, and then we'll see how their sentences turn out. Obviously that's not ethical.

I think there's plenty of room to develop problem sets like the authors of this medical study did, using closed cases or hypotheticals—past cases where you have all of the information with all of its bespoke details (as lawyers like to say).

I think you could learn the most in places where there are high-volume, similar cases—that's true in many eviction cases, which have similar elements, similar potential defenses, and similar outcomes.
The same is true for consumer debt cases. That's also a place where you have the most to gain.

kp.k: Opaque adjudication complicates trials and motivates transparency
kp.d: McCormack identifies judges and juries as additional decision makers whose reasoning complicates legal outcome measurement, notwithstanding written judicial decisions. She suggests studying settings with limited judicial discretion, such as defaults or undefended claims, and considering greater transparency or automation of some decisions, while acknowledging feasibility limits. Leonard anticipates LLM-assisted analysis of judges' own dockets for consistency, fairness, and equity; both frame public confidence as a possible benefit and leave incentives for public-interest use unresolved.
qs: So that's a bit of an issue if you're designing a randomized control trial and you're trying to measure outcomes that involve judges and juries.
Maybe a little bit more openness and sunshine into how decisions are made, or some more automation of how certain decisions are made.

learning more about the insights that an LLM can surface about your decisions, unpacking the similarities and differences across your cases, and whether you are being fair and equitable across those cases seems to me to be something a judge should want to know.
But how do we create drivers in society that incentivize the same for the public?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jen Leonard and Bridget McCormack describe generative AI as a time-saving drafting and creative partner for lawyers' presentations, marketing and business development.
pts.d: Leonard reports that ChatGPT reconstructed approximately 90% of her intended presentation content from sparse slide images and context, leaving relatively minor adjustments. She also reports lawyers using publicly available litigation records and articles to draft client alerts. McCormack identifies both time savings and creative iteration as benefits. These are accounts of current experience, not measured productivity findings or claims that AI autonomously delivers legal advice.

pts.k: The medical researchers' finding, as reported by McCormack, is that GPT-4 alone outperformed physicians on the study's diagnostic tasks, while access to GPT-4 did not significantly improve physician performance.
pts.d: McCormack attributes the research to investigators from Stanford, Beth Israel and UVA, rather than presenting the findings as her own. She describes 50 physicians, randomized between conventional resources and conventional resources plus GPT-4, completing six hypothetical clinical vignettes within 60 minutes, with a separate assessment of the LLM alone. Blinded experts graded the work. She reports a nonsignificant two-point difference between physician groups and significantly better standalone LLM performance. This concerns a medical vignette study, not demonstrated superiority in real patient care or legal work. Leonard separately speculates that subsequent model improvements could make the difference larger; she expresses uncertainty about the precise model version.

pts.k: McCormack predicts that newer lawyers may use AI more ambitiously than established experts because they are more comfortable with the technology and less certain of their own answers.
pts.d: The prediction draws on the medical study discussion and McCormack's experience of initially rejecting a valid procedural argument proposed by clinic students. Leonard connects resistance to expert habits and the dismissal of ideas from non-lawyer disciplines. McCormack also suggests that the profession's dominant business model might not be best suited to the technology. Neither provides comparative legal adoption data or specifies a replacement business model. The concept of 'algorithmic aversion' is attributed in the conversation to Ethan Mollick, not originated by either speaker.

pts.k: Leonard anticipates that shifting some cognitive work to AI could let lawyers serve more people and businesses and devote more attention to human skills.
pts.d: Leonard presents this as an opportunity conditional on lawyers spending less time on work they presently value as intellectually challenging. The proposed reallocation is toward strategic partnership, empathy and problem solving, alongside better services and quicker resolution. McCormack similarly sees substantial scope for improving legal-business efficiency. These are prospective arguments, not quantified forecasts of cost reductions, employment effects or justice-gap closure. The discussion includes unmet legal need, rather than only savings for existing enterprise clients.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack anticipate that clients' prior consultations with ChatGPT will change lawyer-client communication, with newer lawyers potentially advantaged in adapting.
pts.d: Leonard raises a hypothetical solo or small-firm client who arrives with an AI-generated account of legal options and a preferred course of action. McCormack predicts a learning curve and an advantage for new lawyers who learn how to respond from the start of practice. The analogy is physicians handling patients' internet research. The speakers do not establish the accuracy of clients' AI advice or present evidence of how frequently this already occurs.

pts.k: McCormack argues that AI-assisted legal experiments are feasible using closed cases or hypotheticals, particularly in high-volume eviction and consumer-debt matters.
pts.d: McCormack reports using Claude to develop two proposed randomized controlled trials addressing legal diagnosis and decision making. She has not run them and reports no legal performance results. She argues that historical or hypothetical problem sets could avoid ethically assigning live clients to different legal strategies. Similarity and volume make eviction and consumer-debt dockets especially promising; their lack of legal assistance also offers substantial potential benefit. She qualifies the analogy to medical trials because legal outcomes are subjective, context-dependent and influenced by judges and juries.

pts.k: McCormack suggests that analyzing legal language for ambiguity before enactment could reduce subsequent disputes.
pts.d: Building on an example attributed to Adam Unikowski, McCormack makes a conditional prediction that prior analysis of a statute or sentencing guideline could reduce disputes. Leonard supports teaching lawyers to develop consensus around language before laws are created. The claim is about preventive legal work and more predictable rules, not proof that AI eliminates interpretive disagreement. Both acknowledge that ambiguity is difficult to eliminate.

pts.k: Leonard anticipates more detailed AI analysis of judicial decisions that could help judges assess consistency and fairness; McCormack links transparency to public confidence.
pts.d: Leonard describes LLMs as potentially extending existing predictive analytics through more specific comparisons across a judge's docket. She characterizes the capability as emerging, not a demonstrated audit system. McCormack tentatively proposes greater openness or automation of some decisions while acknowledging feasibility limits. Leonard distinguishes private litigators' incentives to improve client outcomes from the unresolved need for incentives to produce public benefits. McCormack's transparency argument encompasses courts and alternative dispute resolution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines a reported medical experiment, personal use experiences, professional anecdotes and speculative legal extrapolations.
pts.d: The medical study is the principal quantitative evidence. The transcript does not give its absolute performance scores, confidence intervals or a full citation. Leonard's approximately 90% drafting estimate is a personal assessment, not a benchmark. McCormack's Claude-assisted trial design establishes an experienced use case, not trial findings. Predictions about expanded service, new-lawyer advantages, fewer disputes and judicial analytics rely on analogy, experience or referenced commentary rather than completed legal studies. Dr. Adam Rodman's views about changing medical cognition and efficiency threatening human interaction are relayed secondhand from his Hard Fork interview; they are not original findings of Leonard or McCormack.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current productivity anecdotes coexist with undated forecasts and explicit limits on transferring medical findings to law.
pts.d: Drafting and research-design uses are described as current in the 2024 episode. McCormack intends to discuss trial designs with law faculty in the coming weeks, without committing to execution. New-lawyer advantages, expanded service and judicial analytics are prospective and have no fixed deadline; the program's '2030 Vision' title is not a prediction date. Conditions include willingness to reconsider expert judgments, greater AI familiarity, suitable cases, meaningful outcome measures and public-benefit incentives. Jurisdictional variation, contested legal meaning, ethical constraints and opaque judicial or jury decision making complicate legal deployment and evaluation. Leonard also suggests legal education may respond more slowly where faculty are not practicing, explicitly labeling her comparison an overgeneralization.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The projected effects reach lawyers, legal educators, clients with and without representation, judicial institutions and the public.
pts.d: Practicing lawyers and law firms gain potential drafting, marketing and analytical efficiencies. Junior lawyers may gain relative advantages in adoption and communication, while established experts may need to reconsider professional habits. Law schools and professional-development providers face questions about training priorities and opportunities to conduct studies. Solo and small-firm lawyers may encounter clients already advised by ChatGPT. Unrepresented people in eviction and consumer-debt cases are identified as especially promising beneficiaries of research and improved assistance. Judges, juries, courts and alternative dispute resolution systems are implicated in proposed transparency and decision-analysis changes. The cross-domain discussion concerns physicians, residents, medical students and patients; it raises the possibility of reallocating clinical cognition to technology and human attention to communication, without resolving whether efficiency pressures would permit that outcome.
